name: servant
intent: Give a group of unrelated classes one shared behaviour by defining it once in a separate servant object whose operations take the serviced objects as parameters, so that none of the classes has to own the behaviour or inherit it from a common ancestor.
problem: Several unrelated classes need the same behaviour and none of them should own it: forcing it into a common superclass distorts the hierarchy (or is impossible when the classes are unrelated, third-party or sealed), duplicating it into every class scatters fixes and invites divergence, and parking it in one of the served classes makes all the others depend on that class and its hierarchy.
context: Behaviour that is common to a group of otherwise unrelated classes but is not intrinsic to any of them - formatting, comparison and ordering, movement and geometry, validation, conversion, protocol handling. It appears most in OO code where inheritance is the only reuse mechanism at hand and the classes must not or cannot share a base class; languages with extension methods, mixin modules, protocol extensions, free functions or extension traits make the same decision by attaching the behaviour to the type instead of to a servant object.
benefits: One home for the behaviour: unrelated classes reuse a single implementation instead of duplicating it, and a fix or policy change lands in exactly one place.

Works where inheritance cannot: classes that must not or cannot share a superclass (different hierarchies, sealed or final types, value types, third-party types reachable through extension facilities) still get the behaviour without a faked base class.
Policy and variation stay outside the serviced types: the servant can be parameterised, swapped or decorated (collation, search order, formatting policy) without touching a single serviced class.

The serviced classes keep their hierarchy and their focus: no shared base is polluted with behaviour that only part of the hierarchy needs, and a new class joins by implementing the usually tiny capability interface.
Testability: the servant is an ordinary collaborator - it can be exercised once against test doubles of the capability interface, and it can be injected where a scenario needs a different policy.
The contract is explicit and minimal: the capability interface states exactly which abilities the behaviour needs, which is far less than the class's whole API (interface segregation).
tradeoffs: Encapsulation tension: the servant can only use what the capability interface exposes, so either the serviced class widens its public surface with accessors that exist for the servant's benefit (weakening its invariants), or the servant is granted privileged access (C++ friend, C# internal) and couples itself to the representation.

Discoverability and feature envy: the behaviour is no longer found by reading the serviced class, and moving domain behaviour out by reflex turns entities into data bags (anemic domain model) whose invariants are only enforced by convention.

A capability interface that is too weak or too generic pushes type tests into the servant; instanceof / isinstance / dynamic_cast chains inside a servant are the signal that the behaviour was polymorphic and belongs in the types (Visitor, double dispatch).

Call sites lose their shape: in languages without extension syntax the operation reads servant.op(a, b) instead of a.op(b), and every caller must obtain the servant (imported, injected, static) before it can serve anything.
Static or utility-class servants are not substitutable: they cannot be mocked, configured per scenario, or replaced at runtime, so tests end up wired to the real implementation.

State is easy to put in the wrong place: a servant that accumulates per-client state becomes a hidden global (thread-safety, unbounded growth), while statelessness pushes every input through a parameter list.

Foreign serviced types may still need an adapter: when the language requires a nominal interface and the class cannot be changed, each third-party type needs a wrapper before the servant can serve it.

One algorithm constraint: if different serviced types genuinely need different variants of the operation, Servant forces you to either widen the capability interface with type tags or type-test inside the servant — Visitor or double dispatch is the correct escape hatch. Servant shines only when one algorithm applies uniformly.

participants.responsibility: Holds the shared behaviour and whatever policy or configuration state belongs to the service. It carries no serviced-object state; its operations take serviced objects as parameters and work only through the capability interface (unless it is explicitly granted privileged access).

Declares the minimal abilities the servant requires from everything it serves (Movable, Comparable, sort.Interface, IComparable). Declared on the servant's side, it tells serviced classes exactly what to provide and keeps the servant independent of their concrete types.

An otherwise unrelated class (or several unrelated hierarchies) that implements the capability interface and is handed to the servant; it does not own the behaviour, does not inherit it, and in the caller-driven form does not even know the servant exists.

Knows both sides, obtains the servant and passes the serviced objects to it. In the second published form the serviced object itself plays this role: it holds a reference to the servant and forwards the request, so callers see only the serviced class.

use_cases: Geometric services over heterogeneous shapes: MoveServant or GeometryTools working through a small Movable/HasBounds interface (getPosition/setPosition) across unrelated Rectangle, Circle, Triangle — the canonical GoF example.

Formatting and serialisation for unrelated domain objects: rendering as JSON, CSV, XML, display lines — each class exposes only the fields the formatter needs through a minimal capability interface, keeping the domain model uncluttered.

GUI toolkit hit-testing and rendering: a Renderer or HitTestServant operating through a Drawable/Bounds interface across unrelated UI widgets without polluting their class hierarchies. Production retained-UI frameworks (e.g., Estella's UISystem) separate layout computation from hit-testing into dedicated service objects that iterate over heterogeneous widget registries, applying the same point-in-rect or OBB tests uniformly via a minimal Transform/Interactable interface.

Game engine cross-entity behaviour: collision detection, physics resolution, movement or raycasting servants over heterogeneous entities (Player, Enemy, Item, Prop) through a common Transform or PhysicsBody interface. Engines like Simulant expose a PhysicsService that performs ray_cast queries across all registered physics bodies, while the entities themselves implement no physics logic — they only expose their world-space position and collider geometry through a minimal interface.

Cross-cutting audit, tracing and validation: an AuditServant applying the same logging, access-validation or consistency-check over many unrelated types through an Auditable/Validatable interface, without embedding the concern in each class.

Sorting and comparison policies across heterogeneous collections: a Comparator or Collator servant applying locale-aware collation or custom ordering through a Comparable interface implemented by otherwise unrelated types.

Interaction systems in game engines: PlayerController or InteractionComponent in Unreal-style architectures acts as a servant that scans for nearby interactable entities via a physics overlap query and calls Interact() on whichever entity satisfies the URogueInteractionInterface — the same controller serves any entity implementing the interface, from chests to doors to enemies, without those entities inheriting from a shared base.

Document export and cross-format rendering: a DocumentExporter servant applies the same serialisation logic to unrelated domain objects (Invoice, Report, Receipt) that each expose only the fields needed for the target format, keeping the domain classes free of export-specific code.

Protocol handling and codec operations: a CodecServant encoding or decoding heterogeneous message types through a minimal Serializable/Encodable interface, common in network middleware and RPC frameworks where message classes must not be polluted by transport-layer concerns.

Go standard-library sorting: the collection type implements the three-method capability interface sort.Interface (Len, Less, Swap) and the servant sort.Sort/stable.Sort performs the entire algorithm against that interface — the elements and the slice's own domain behaviour are untouched, and any unrelated type joins by supplying the three methods. Since Go 1.21 the stdlib also offers the generic free-function alternative (slices.SortFunc, cmp.Compare), the direct-attachment form the same guidance recommends when no policy state must be carried.

.NET comparison services: List<T>.Sort(IComparer<T>) and SortedDictionary<TKey,TValue> drive ordering through the IComparer<T> servant so unrelated element types need no shared base or ordering method of their own; Comparer<T>.Default is the shipped fallback that delegates to IComparable<T> only when the element does own the comparison, and StringComparer supplies substitutable culture/case policies — the capability interface (IComparable<T>) and the swappable policy servant (IComparer<T>) stay cleanly separated.
avoid_when: A shared base class or interface already owns the behaviour, or you control the classes: put the operation (or a default method) there and skip the extra role.
The behaviour uses the type's representation to preserve its invariants: keep it in the class (C++ Core Guidelines C.4) - a servant reaching in through accessors externalises the invariant.
The variation is per type rather than shared: use polymorphism - Strategy, Template Method, Visitor, double dispatch - instead of a servant that type-tests its arguments.
Only one class is served and it can own the behaviour: a method on that class is simpler than a servant plus a capability interface.

The serviced types are third-party and the language demands a nominal interface (Java, C++): you would write an Adapter per type before the servant can serve it, which usually costs more than the duplication it removes.
anti_patterns: Utils/Helper god class: a servant that collects every operation which lacked a home ('StringUtils', 'Helper', 'Manager') instead of one cohesive service; if the name needs the word Helper, the cohesion is missing.

Anemic domain model by reflex: domain behaviour is moved out of the objects into servants so entities become data bags, and their invariants become optional because external code now drives them through the capability interface's setters.

Type-testing servant: instanceof / isinstance / dynamic_cast / switch-on-type chains inside the servant because the capability interface was too weak - the polymorphic behaviour should live in the types.
Static-everything servant: a utility class of static methods reaching into mutable globals or singletons, impossible to vary per scenario and painful to test.

Installing the servant into the serviced class: monkey-patching the prototype (JavaScript, Ruby) to add the methods globally, shadowing existing members and breaking on the next upgrade of the patched type.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: shared behaviour gets its own object instead of being duplicated in every class or forced into a common base.
Composition over inheritance: the serviced objects collaborate with a servant instead of inheriting from one.
Interface segregation: the servant requires only the minimal capability interface it needs, not the serviced class's whole API.
Dependency inversion: the serviced classes depend on a small abstraction (the capability interface), and the servant depends on that abstraction rather than on concrete serviced types.
DRY and single responsibility: one implementation of the shared behaviour, one reason for the servant to change.
Open/closed: new serviced types join by implementing the capability interface, and new behaviour means a new servant rather than edits to the serviced classes.
best_practices: Name the servant after the service it performs (MoveServant, Formatter, Comparator, PhysicsService) and keep it cohesive — one well-defined capability; never let it become the place where everything without a home accumulates. A servant that needs the word Helper in its name has already lost its cohesion.

Keep the capability interface role-shaped and minimal — name it after the ability the servant needs (Movable, Comparable, sort.Interface, Interactable) rather than exposing the class's state wholesale; resist adding accessors that exist solely to serve one servant.

Prefer the language's direct attachment facility (extension methods/functions, protocol extensions, mixin modules, free functions, extension traits) over hand-rolling a servant class. Reserve the explicit Servant object form when the servant carries policy state that must be substituted in tests, or when multiple cooperating servants need to share the same serviced objects.

Make the servant stateless with respect to the serviced objects so it can be shared freely and is thread-safe; per-object state belongs in the serviced objects. A servant that accumulates per-client state is a hidden shared global with all its thread-safety and unbounded-growth problems.

Depend on an injected servant (or a servant factory) rather than a static helper whenever the behaviour touches I/O, the clock, configuration or anything a test must control. Even a stateless servant should be injectable so tests can substitute a mock or a test-specific subclass.

Treat the appearance of instanceof / isinstance / dynamic_cast / type-switch chains inside a servant as a hard design smell — the capability interface was too weak and the operation is genuinely polymorphic. Migrate to Visitor with double dispatch: the element types stay unchanged, the visitor class grows one method per element type.

When the behaviour is intrinsic (invariant-preserving, representation-dependent, tied to the class's core responsibility), leave it in the class. Servant is for behaviour the class should not own because it is shared by unrelated classes or would distort the hierarchy.

For stateless utility-style servants that are pure functions over data (geometry, formatting, comparison), prefer the language's native extension facility. For servants that carry policy, configuration or mutable state, use the explicit object form with a capability interface so the servant can be mocked and configured.

Document the two-sided contract explicitly: what the servant requires from the capability interface, and which classes it currently serves. When a new servant requires a change to the capability interface, treat that as a signal to re-examine whether all current servants really belong to the same behavioural family.

When the serviced types are third-party and the language requires a nominal interface (Java, C# before default interface methods), count the adapters before committing: each served class needs a wrapper implementing the capability interface, which may cost more than the duplication the servant removes. In such cases prefer the language's extension facility or a code-generation step to automate the adapter.

Limit the number of unrelated capability interfaces a servant requires; a Movable plus a Scalable plus a Serialisable interface on the same servant signals the servant is doing too much and should be split into separate servants with single responsibilities.

Evolve the servant, not the capability interface: adding a method to the interface is a breaking change for every implementer — including third-party types you wrapped in adapters — so when a new operation needs an extra ability, add a new servant that requires a sub-interface, pass the extra input as a parameter, or (Java 8+, C# 8+) add a default method whose body can be derived from the existing contract.

Do not name a class Servant: the bare word is a reserved term of art elsewhere — in CORBA/POA a Servant (org.omg.PortableServer.Servant) is the server-side object that does own the behaviour, close to the inverse of this pattern — and readers will import the wrong model. Name the class after the service it performs (MoveServant, PhysicsService, DocumentExporter).
sources: Pecinovský, Pavlíčková & Pavlíček, 'Let’s Modify the Objects First Approach into Design-Patterns-First', ITiCSE 2006 — https://doi.org/10.1145/1140124.1140175 — the original published description of Servant as a named pattern; the paper explicitly identifies Servant as 'another type of the design pattern Command' and uses it in the second lecture of an OOP course to introduce interfaces as a formalisation of the servant's requirements.
iluwatar, 'Servant Pattern in Java', Java Design Patterns — https://java-design-patterns.com/patterns/servant/

Kapoor, 'Visitor vs Servant vs Command patterns', Stack Overflow (accepted answer, 2015) — https://stackoverflow.com/questions/31986332/visitor-vs-servant-vs-command-patterns — definitive community answer establishing the one-algorithm (Servant) vs N-algorithms-via-double-dispatch (Visitor) distinction.

HandWiki, 'Servant (design pattern)' — https://handwiki.org/wiki/Servant_(design_pattern) — step-by-step design procedure including identifying servant operations, defining the capability interface, and implementing serviced classes.

Kinanu, 'Design Patterns — Servant', Medium — https://medium.com/@kinan.qutaibi/design-patterns-servant-7f8f30e5f924 — practical walkthrough with C# code showing the MoveServant/IMovable canonical example.

Simulant Engine, 'PhysicsService Raycasting' — https://simulant-engine.appspot.com/docs/physics/raycasting.md — production game engine documentation showing PhysicsService as a servant performing ray_cast queries across heterogeneous physics bodies through a minimal contact/result interface.

Matthew Berger, 'Build your own retained UI (part 2): layout and interaction' (2026) — https://matthewberger.dev/articles/posts/build-your-own-retained-ui-layout-interaction/ — detailed walkthrough of a retained UI framework's layout system and interaction system as separate servant-style services operating over a heterogeneous widget hierarchy.

Gaetano Tonzuso, 'Architectural Refactoring: Player Controllers, Pure C++ Interfaces, and Real-Time Targeting in Unreal Engine 5', Medium (2026) — https://medium.com/@gaetano.tonzuso/architectural-refactoring-player-controllers-pure-c-interfaces-and-real-time-targeting-in-6e98453137ab — demonstrates a PlayerController-as-servant interacting with any entity implementing IRogueInteractionInterface across the game world.
Go team, 'sort package' — https://pkg.go.dev/sort — sort.Interface (Len/Less/Swap) as a shipped capability interface and sort.Sort as the servant that runs the whole ordering algorithm against it.

Go team, 'Go 1.21 Release Notes' — https://go.dev/doc/go1.21 — introduces the slices and cmp packages, the generic free-function alternatives that supersede hand-rolled sort.Interface servants when no policy state is carried.

Microsoft, 'IComparer<T> Interface (System.Collections.Generic)' — https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.icomparer-1?view=net-10.0 — comparison servant consumed by List<T>.Sort/SortedDictionary, with Comparer<T>.Default falling back to the element's own IComparable<T>.

Oracle, 'Evolving Interfaces' (Java Tutorials) — https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/IandI/nogrow.html — why adding a method to an interface breaks all implementers and the sanctioned workarounds (sub-interface, default method): the lifecycle constraint on any capability interface.

Oracle, 'Servant (org.omg.PortableServer)' (Java SE 8 API) — https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/org/omg/PortableServer/Servant.html — the colliding CORBA/POA meaning of 'servant' (the server-side object that implements the operations), which is why pattern classes should be named after their service.

Jason Seifer, 'Beware of "service objects" in Rails' — https://www.codewithjason.com/rails-service-objects/ — the external critique this pattern must answer: -er/-or service classes as procedural code in disguise, driving the domain toward Fowler's anemic domain model when behaviour is externalised by reflex.

related_patterns_notes.command: Command wraps a request, its arguments and its receiver into an autonomous storable/queueable/undoable object; Servant performs an operation immediately on serviced objects passed as parameters. Command decouples sender from receiver across time (the request outlives the call); Servant is synchronous and stateless. Both factor behaviour out of the primary class, but Command carries state for later execution while Servant just delivers the result right now; contrast: Use Command when you need to store, queue, undo or replay operations; use Servant when the operation is stateless and executed immediately on heterogeneous objects.
related_patterns_notes.strategy: Strategy encapsulates a swappable algorithm inside the object that uses it; Servant encapsulates the algorithm in an external object that the caller passes serviced objects into. Both externalise behaviour, but Strategy selects which algorithm runs inside one context, while Servant applies one algorithm uniformly across many unrelated objects; contrast: Use Strategy when you need to interchange the algorithm inside a single context (e.g., different sort algorithms); use Servant when unrelated classes all need the same behaviour applied.
related_patterns_notes.visitor: Visitor applies N related algorithms — one per concrete serviced type — via double dispatch: the element calls back into the visitor with its own type, selecting the right overload. Servant applies a single algorithm uniformly; no type-based dispatch inside the servant. The defining distinction: Servant = one algorithm for all types; Visitor = N algorithms (one per type). The canonical test: if your servant contains instanceof/dynamic_cast/type-switch chains, the operation is polymorphic and Visitor is the correct pattern; contrast: Use Servant when the same algorithm works identically for all serviced types; use Visitor when different types need different behaviours, or when the object structure is stable but operations over it grow frequently.
related_patterns_notes.decorator: Decorator wraps a single object to add responsibilities (logging, caching, retry) dynamically at runtime, preserving the wrapped object's interface. Servant serves multiple unrelated objects with shared behaviour without wrapping any of them — the serviced objects are passed as parameters, not held as state. Decorator modifies one object's behaviour from the outside; Servant centralises behaviour that applies to many objects; contrast: Use Decorator to add optional layered responsibilities to one object; use Servant when behaviour belongs to none of the served objects and must be shared across many.
related_patterns_notes.delegation: Delegation is the broad mechanism of forwarding a request to another object; Servant is a specific form where the servant holds no serviced-object state and the serviced objects do not know they are being served. Simple delegation (e.g., a Proxy forwarding calls) differs in that the client typically believes it is talking to the delegate directly; contrast: Delegation is the mechanical act of forwarding; Servant is a design pattern that formalises when and why the forwarding relationship exists. Not all delegation is Servant-shaped.
related_patterns_notes.adapter: Adapter converts the interface of a class into one a client expects, enabling interoperability. Servant and Adapter compose naturally: when the serviced classes are third-party and do not implement the capability interface, each class needs an Adapter before the Servant can serve it. The Adapter bridges the gap; the Servant provides the shared behaviour; contrast: Use Adapter to make incompatible interfaces work together; use Servant to centralise shared behaviour across classes that already share a compatible interface.
related_patterns_notes.extension-interface: Extension interface (the Capability Interface pattern) is the contract side of Servant — it is the minimal interface the serviced classes must implement so the Servant can operate on them. Extension interface and Servant are two halves of the same design decision: one defines the required abilities, the other implements the behaviour against those abilities; contrast: Extension interface is a role interface on the serviced side; Servant is the implementation of the behaviour. They always appear together in a correct Servant design.
